title: Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed
content:
When building Maestro's hook system, I had to make a design choice: if the app isn't running when Claude Code fires a permission hook, what should happen?

Option A: **Fail-closed**. The hook returns an error. Claude Code blocks the operation. Nothing runs without explicit approval.

Option B: **Fail-open**. The hook returns "allow". Claude Code proceeds as if Maestro approved it. The operation runs.

I went with fail-open.

---

The reasoning: the primary use case for Maestro is oversight, not blocking. If someone has Claude Code running and Maestro isn't open, the most likely reason is that they forgot to start Maestro — not that they want to block all tool use indefinitely.

Fail-closed in this case would mean: every time the app crashes, or the user forgets to start it, all Claude sessions grind to a halt. The feature becomes a liability instead of a convenience.

---

Fail-open vs fail-closed is fundamentally a question about which failure mode is more acceptable.

For authentication systems: fail-closed is the right answer. If your auth service goes down, you don't want to let everyone in by default. The cost of letting the wrong person through is catastrophic.

For permission oversight tools: fail-open is more defensible. The cost of blocking legitimate work because your UI isn't running is high. The cost of running an operation without manual approval is... usually fine, since you set up the tool in the first place.

---

There's a related concept: **graceful degradation**. Instead of binary fail-open/fail-closed, some systems fall back to a simpler mode.

For Maestro, a graceful degradation might look like: if the app isn't running, apply a basic rule set (allow read-only operations, deny shell commands with destructive flags). More conservative than full fail-open, less disruptive than fail-closed.

That's a reasonable next iteration. But for the initial version, fail-open with a clear log entry is the pragmatic choice.

---

The hook script I wrote does this:

```sh
if [ -n "$RESP" ]; then
    printf '%s' "$RESP"   # Maestro responded — use its decision
else
    printf '{"decision":{"behavior":"allow"}}'   # Maestro not running — allow
fi
```

Six lines. The policy is explicit. Anyone reading the script immediately understands the fallback behavior.

---

Make the failure behavior as legible as the success behavior.

If you can't answer "what happens when this component is down?" before shipping, you haven't finished the design.
